# Forensic Dossier — Fox Corporation (FOXA, Class A voting shares)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Six quarters of earnings calls (fiscal Q3 2025 through fiscal Q3 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory, then re-anchored to a deal announced after the last call — Fox's June 15, 2026 agreement to acquire Roku for about $22 billion. That deal changes the conclusion, and the dossier says so plainly.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

For most of the period covered by these calls, Fox told one of the cleanest stories in legacy media, and the numbers backed it up. The arc, in management's own framing, was "differentiated and focused": lean into the two ad categories that are still growing — live sports and live news — plus a free, ad-supported streaming service (Tubi) that scaled into real money. Across the six calls the chief executive, Lachlan Murdoch, hit the same notes with rising confidence: record Super Bowl (over $800 million of gross ad revenue, "the most watched telecast in U.S. history"), Fox News holding "over 60% share of the cable news audience," Tubi crossing $1.1 billion in revenue and reaching profitability, and "the strongest advertising market we have seen for some time" (fiscal Q1 2026, repeated in Q2).

Two new growth drivers were introduced and pushed hard. First, **Fox One**, the direct-to-consumer streaming app launched August 21, 2025 at $19.99 per month, pitched at "cord-cutters and cord-nevers" with explicit promises of no cannibalization of the traditional cable bundle. By fiscal Q3 2026 management said churn was "much lower than we had expected" and "over half of the viewership on Fox One is news." Second, the **sports-betting optionality** — a 2.5% equity stake in Flutter (worth roughly $700 million) and a call option over 18.6% of FanDuel (intrinsic value management pegged at $2.1–2.8 billion, "about 6 to 7 dollars per share … which we don't think is reflected today").

The capital-allocation story was, until the very end, the spine of the bull case: a "fortress-like balance sheet," a $5 billion buyback authorization increase (August 2025), and a $1.5 billion accelerated share repurchase (October 2025), with cumulative buybacks reaching over one-third of shares outstanding. Management repeatedly said it had "a very high internal benchmark for the use of our capital" and would "reject out of hand" any imprudent deal.

**That last claim did not survive contact with reality.** On June 15, 2026 — a month after the final call in this set — Fox announced it would acquire Roku for $160.00 per share, about $22 billion of enterprise value, paying $96 cash and 0.9693 Fox Class A shares per Roku share. That is roughly $15 billion of cash, about 152 million newly issued Fox shares, up to $12 billion of bridge financing and $8.3 billion of new debt, lifting pro-forma net leverage to about 2.8 times. The market cut the stock roughly 17–18% on the day to a fresh 52-week low near $50. The "disciplined, fortress balance sheet, return-the-cash" narrative that ran through every one of these calls was abandoned in a single transaction.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record free cash flow … best year yet" (fiscal Q4 2025) | Fiscal 2025 free cash flow grew ~100% year-over-year to about $3 billion; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow about $2.36 billion as of March 2026; price-to-free-cash-flow about 7.7x | Matches. Real cash generation, genuinely cheap on a cash basis. |
| "EBITDA growth of 26% to $3.6 billion … adjusted EPS growth of 39%" (fiscal Q4 2025) | Five-year trajectory: revenue $12.9B (2021) → $16.3B (2025); net income $2.15B → $2.26B; EPS $3.61 → $4.91. Fiscal 2025 was a clear step-up | Matches, but note the step-up rode the Super Bowl and a record political-ad cycle — both non-recurring. |
| "Subscriber declines remaining below 7% … a very healthy trend" | The core cord-cutting drag is real and ongoing; management's own number shows pay-TV erosion of roughly 6.5% a year. "Healthy" here means "decelerating decline," not growth | Richer story than the numbers justify. A shrinking base decelerating is still shrinking. |
| "Fortress-like balance sheet … we will continue repurchasing our shares" (every call) | True through March 2026: net debt about $3.0 billion (total debt $6.61B minus cash $3.60B) on $3.6B EBITDA — very modest leverage | Was true; the Roku deal inverts it to ~2.8x pro-forma leverage and converts cash-return into cash-out. |
| "We have a very high internal benchmark … reject out of hand anything imprudent" (fiscal Q4 2025) | The same management then agreed to pay ~$22 billion for Roku — a company whose platform thesis is strategically logical but whose price drew an immediate ~17% punishment and a Barclays price-target cut | Did not hold up. The clearest gap between word and deed in the file. |
| Gross margin "33.1% (contracting)"; margin "-0.41 standard deviations vs historical peak" | Gross margin is sliding even as revenue grows — the cost of sports rights and streaming investment is climbing faster than the top line | Matches the bear read: this is an operationally fine but margin-pressured business, not a widening-moat compounder. |
| Insider conviction | Screener's grant-inflated buy ratio is misleading; the clean open-market record is **0 buys versus 10 sells (about 1.4 million shares)** | No insider is putting personal cash in at these levels. A quiet negative. |

The forensic headline: the operating business does roughly what management says it does — it throws off real cash and leads its two best ad verticals. But the latest-quarter optics are softening (latest-quarter EPS down 49% year-over-year as the Super Bowl lapped; trailing diluted EPS $3.79 versus the $4.91 fiscal-year figure), and the capital-allocation discipline that anchored the investment case has just been spent on a large, debt-and-stock-funded acquisition.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Rising, then a regime change the calls never captured.** Through all six transcripts the tone is offensive and increasingly assured — "the most robust advertising market we have seen for some time" (fiscal Q1 2026), "in almost every way, it has exceeded our expectations" on Fox One (fiscal Q3 2026), "record EBITDA this fiscal year" (fiscal Q3 2026). Guidance got *more* specific over time, not less: digital investment was walked down from "around $350 million" to "comfortably inside the $290 million" as Tubi reached profitability — a credibility-builder. There is no defensive pivot in the language; right to the last call management is talking growth, the World Cup, and the midterm political-ad cycle.

The tell the calls *do* contain, in hindsight, is the steadily louder drumbeat on mergers and acquisitions. By fiscal Q1 2026 the chief executive moved from "we don't have anything to announce" to "**we would expect to be doing more M&A over the coming period** … M&A is going to be an important part of our growth going forward." The market should have read that as a warning that the buyback-forever thesis had a shelf life. The Roku deal is the cash-out that language foreshadowed.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High on operations, newly questionable on capital allocation.** On the numbers management has delivered repeatedly — the screener shows a beat in 7 of 7 reported quarters, and the specific in-year guide-downs on digital investment came true in the company's favor (less spend, faster Tubi profitability). On operating promises, this is a Medium-to-High credibility management team.

But guidance credibility is not only about hitting numbers; it is about whether the stated *strategy* holds. Management spent six calls promising disciplined capital return and a high deal-benchmark, then signed a transformational acquisition that the market judged value-destructive in the near term. That does not make them liars — strategies can legitimately change — but it does mean the single most load-bearing promise in the bull case (return cash, stay un-levered) is no longer operative. Net of both: **Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three themes recur in the Q&A, and they map almost perfectly onto where the story later broke:

1. **"What will you do with the balance sheet / will there be M&A?"** Jessica Reif Cohen (Bank of America) and others pressed this in nearly every call. Management deflected — "nothing on the table now" — while signaling appetite. Analysts were right to worry; this is exactly the lever that just moved against shareholders.
2. **The FanDuel option timing.** Steven Cahall (Wells Fargo) and others repeatedly asked when Fox would exercise. Management's answer never changed: a multi-state licensing process, no rush, "over four years to do that." The takeaway is that this $2–3 billion of optionality is real but *not* a near-term catalyst — it is years away and gated by regulators.
3. **Fox One cannibalization and the affiliate/FCC relationship.** Analysts probed whether the streaming app would erode the cable bundle and whether reverse-compensation economics with affiliates were at risk. Management gave reassuring, non-committal answers ("no noticeable cannibalization").

What analysts were *not* asking about, because management gave no hint of it, was a $22 billion living-room platform acquisition. The biggest risk in the file was the one the calls were silent on.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 The Roku acquisition: ~$22 billion, $15 billion cash, ~152 million new shares (~27% of the combined company to Roku holders), pro-forma leverage to ~2.8x, accretion to free cash flow per share not promised until the *second full year* after closing. The market's ~17–18% one-day cut is the cleanest red flag possible.
🔴 Open-market insider activity: zero buys, ten sells (~1.4 million shares). No insider is leaning in.
🔴 Gross margin contracting while sports-rights costs climb; latest-quarter EPS down 49% year-over-year on the Super Bowl lap.
🔴 The thesis rested on a "fortress balance sheet" that no longer exists.

🟢 Genuine, large free cash flow (~$2.4 billion trailing) at a single-digit multiple — the deep-value starting point is real.
🟢 Tubi reached profitability ahead of plan; Fox One churn below expectations; both are credible, self-funded growth assets.
🟢 Two best-positioned ad verticals (live sports, live news) that are net beneficiaries of cord-cutting, not victims of it the way scripted-cable peers are.
🟢 Embedded sports-betting optionality (Flutter stake + FanDuel option) worth a stated ~$6–7 per share that the market does not credit.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important hidden signal is the **escalation of M&A language** described in Section 3 — management told you the cash was going to be deployed inorganically, and the market simply did not price the size or the target. A second, subtler signal is the **shift in how "distribution revenue" is defined**: starting in fiscal Q1 2026 the company folded Fox One subscription fees into the same line as traditional affiliate fees, which flatters the "distribution revenue grew 3–4%" headline by blending a growing new product with a declining old one. It is not deceptive — they disclose it — but it means the reported distribution growth overstates the health of the legacy cable affiliate business underneath.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** Fox is mid-transformation from a disciplined, cash-returning, focused-content operator into a content-plus-distribution-platform company via a large, leveraging, dilutive acquisition. The operating business is stable-to-strong; the capital-allocation posture has flipped.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** the entire deep-value case here was built on a fortress balance sheet and relentless buyback at a single-digit free-cash-flow multiple. That foundation was removed on June 15, 2026. Any position must be underwritten on the *post-Roku* Fox — higher debt, ~27% more shares in the float once the deal closes, free-cash-flow-per-share accretion that is years out, and integration risk against a platform (Roku) the market itself is skeptical Fox overpaid for. The cheapness is now partly a *deal-uncertainty* discount, not purely a legacy-media fear-print.

**Economic moat:** NARROW and, on the legacy side, ERODING. Fox's edge is an intangible-brand moat in live news (Fox News's audience is genuinely sticky and hard to replicate) plus must-have live-sports rights — both real, both why Fox is the *least* threatened legacy-media name. But return on invested capital is only about 10%, gross margin is contracting, and the affiliate base is shrinking 6–7% a year. This is a narrow brand-and-rights moat sitting on a structurally declining linear-distribution base, with returns that are decent but not widening. The Roku deal is precisely an attempt to buy a way off that declining base — which tells you management agrees the legacy moat is eroding.

**Secular threat:** MATERIAL (not terminal). The structural force is cord-cutting and the migration of viewing and advertising from linear to streaming. Fox is better positioned than any peer because live sports and live news travel to streaming with their value largely intact, and Tubi/Fox One are credible bridges. But the legacy cable-affiliate cash engine is in secular decline, and the Roku acquisition is a bet-the-balance-sheet response to it. The cheapness is therefore a mix of a legitimate fear-print on a cash-generative franchise and a genuine question about whether a $22 billion deal at ~2.8x leverage is the right answer.

# Forensic Dossier — Fox Corporation (FOXA, Class A voting shares)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Six quarters of earnings calls (fiscal Q3 2025 through fiscal Q3 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory, then re-anchored to a deal announced after the last call — Fox's June 15, 2026 agreement to acquire Roku for about $22 billion. That deal changes the conclusion, and the dossier says so plainly.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

For most of the period covered by these calls, Fox told one of the cleanest stories in legacy media, and the numbers backed it up. The arc, in management's own framing, was "differentiated and focused": lean into the two ad categories that are still growing — live sports and live news — plus a free, ad-supported streaming service (Tubi) that scaled into real money. Across the six calls the chief executive, Lachlan Murdoch, hit the same notes with rising confidence: record Super Bowl (over $800 million of gross ad revenue, "the most watched telecast in U.S. history"), Fox News holding "over 60% share of the cable news audience," Tubi crossing $1.1 billion in revenue and reaching profitability, and "the strongest advertising market we have seen for some time" (fiscal Q1 2026, repeated in Q2).

Two new growth drivers were introduced and pushed hard. First, **Fox One**, the direct-to-consumer streaming app launched August 21, 2025 at $19.99 per month, pitched at "cord-cutters and cord-nevers" with explicit promises of no cannibalization of the traditional cable bundle. By fiscal Q3 2026 management said churn was "much lower than we had expected" and "over half of the viewership on Fox One is news." Second, the **sports-betting optionality** — a 2.5% equity stake in Flutter (worth roughly $700 million) and a call option over 18.6% of FanDuel (intrinsic value management pegged at $2.1–2.8 billion, "about 6 to 7 dollars per share … which we don't think is reflected today").

The capital-allocation story was, until the very end, the spine of the bull case: a "fortress-like balance sheet," a $5 billion buyback authorization increase (August 2025), and a $1.5 billion accelerated share repurchase (October 2025), with cumulative buybacks reaching over one-third of shares outstanding. Management repeatedly said it had "a very high internal benchmark for the use of our capital" and would "reject out of hand" any imprudent deal.

**That last claim did not survive contact with reality.** On June 15, 2026 — a month after the final call in this set — Fox announced it would acquire Roku for $160.00 per share, about $22 billion of enterprise value, paying $96 cash and 0.9693 Fox Class A shares per Roku share. That is roughly $15 billion of cash, about 152 million newly issued Fox shares, up to $12 billion of bridge financing and $8.3 billion of new debt, lifting pro-forma net leverage to about 2.8 times. The market cut the stock roughly 17–18% on the day to a fresh 52-week low near $50. The "disciplined, fortress balance sheet, return-the-cash" narrative that ran through every one of these calls was abandoned in a single transaction.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record free cash flow … best year yet" (fiscal Q4 2025) | Fiscal 2025 free cash flow grew ~100% year-over-year to about $3 billion; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow about $2.36 billion as of March 2026; price-to-free-cash-flow about 7.7x | Matches. Real cash generation, genuinely cheap on a cash basis. |
| "EBITDA growth of 26% to $3.6 billion … adjusted EPS growth of 39%" (fiscal Q4 2025) | Five-year trajectory: revenue $12.9B (2021) → $16.3B (2025); net income $2.15B → $2.26B; EPS $3.61 → $4.91. Fiscal 2025 was a clear step-up | Matches, but note the step-up rode the Super Bowl and a record political-ad cycle — both non-recurring. |
| "Subscriber declines remaining below 7% … a very healthy trend" | The core cord-cutting drag is real and ongoing; management's own number shows pay-TV erosion of roughly 6.5% a year. "Healthy" here means "decelerating decline," not growth | Richer story than the numbers justify. A shrinking base decelerating is still shrinking. |
| "Fortress-like balance sheet … we will continue repurchasing our shares" (every call) | True through March 2026: net debt about $3.0 billion (total debt $6.61B minus cash $3.60B) on $3.6B EBITDA — very modest leverage | Was true; the Roku deal inverts it to ~2.8x pro-forma leverage and converts cash-return into cash-out. |
| "We have a very high internal benchmark … reject out of hand anything imprudent" (fiscal Q4 2025) | The same management then agreed to pay ~$22 billion for Roku — a company whose platform thesis is strategically logical but whose price drew an immediate ~17% punishment and a Barclays price-target cut | Did not hold up. The clearest gap between word and deed in the file. |
| Gross margin "33.1% (contracting)"; margin "-0.41 standard deviations vs historical peak" | Gross margin is sliding even as revenue grows — the cost of sports rights and streaming investment is climbing faster than the top line | Matches the bear read: this is an operationally fine but margin-pressured business, not a widening-moat compounder. |
| Insider conviction | Screener's grant-inflated buy ratio is misleading; the clean open-market record is **0 buys versus 10 sells (about 1.4 million shares)** | No insider is putting personal cash in at these levels. A quiet negative. |

The forensic headline: the operating business does roughly what management says it does — it throws off real cash and leads its two best ad verticals. But the latest-quarter optics are softening (latest-quarter EPS down 49% year-over-year as the Super Bowl lapped; trailing diluted EPS $3.79 versus the $4.91 fiscal-year figure), and the capital-allocation discipline that anchored the investment case has just been spent on a large, debt-and-stock-funded acquisition.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Rising, then a regime change the calls never captured.** Through all six transcripts the tone is offensive and increasingly assured — "the most robust advertising market we have seen for some time" (fiscal Q1 2026), "in almost every way, it has exceeded our expectations" on Fox One (fiscal Q3 2026), "record EBITDA this fiscal year" (fiscal Q3 2026). Guidance got *more* specific over time, not less: digital investment was walked down from "around $350 million" to "comfortably inside the $290 million" as Tubi reached profitability — a credibility-builder. There is no defensive pivot in the language; right to the last call management is talking growth, the World Cup, and the midterm political-ad cycle.

The tell the calls *do* contain, in hindsight, is the steadily louder drumbeat on mergers and acquisitions. By fiscal Q1 2026 the chief executive moved from "we don't have anything to announce" to "**we would expect to be doing more M&A over the coming period** … M&A is going to be an important part of our growth going forward." The market should have read that as a warning that the buyback-forever thesis had a shelf life. The Roku deal is the cash-out that language foreshadowed.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High on operations, newly questionable on capital allocation.** On the numbers management has delivered repeatedly — the screener shows a beat in 7 of 7 reported quarters, and the specific in-year guide-downs on digital investment came true in the company's favor (less spend, faster Tubi profitability). On operating promises, this is a Medium-to-High credibility management team.

But guidance credibility is not only about hitting numbers; it is about whether the stated *strategy* holds. Management spent six calls promising disciplined capital return and a high deal-benchmark, then signed a transformational acquisition that the market judged value-destructive in the near term. That does not make them liars — strategies can legitimately change — but it does mean the single most load-bearing promise in the bull case (return cash, stay un-levered) is no longer operative. Net of both: **Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three themes recur in the Q&A, and they map almost perfectly onto where the story later broke:

1. **"What will you do with the balance sheet / will there be M&A?"** Jessica Reif Cohen (Bank of America) and others pressed this in nearly every call. Management deflected — "nothing on the table now" — while signaling appetite. Analysts were right to worry; this is exactly the lever that just moved against shareholders.
2. **The FanDuel option timing.** Steven Cahall (Wells Fargo) and others repeatedly asked when Fox would exercise. Management's answer never changed: a multi-state licensing process, no rush, "over four years to do that." The takeaway is that this $2–3 billion of optionality is real but *not* a near-term catalyst — it is years away and gated by regulators.
3. **Fox One cannibalization and the affiliate/FCC relationship.** Analysts probed whether the streaming app would erode the cable bundle and whether reverse-compensation economics with affiliates were at risk. Management gave reassuring, non-committal answers ("no noticeable cannibalization").

What analysts were *not* asking about, because management gave no hint of it, was a $22 billion living-room platform acquisition. The biggest risk in the file was the one the calls were silent on.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 The Roku acquisition: ~$22 billion, $15 billion cash, ~152 million new shares (~27% of the combined company to Roku holders), pro-forma leverage to ~2.8x, accretion to free cash flow per share not promised until the *second full year* after closing. The market's ~17–18% one-day cut is the cleanest red flag possible.
🔴 Open-market insider activity: zero buys, ten sells (~1.4 million shares). No insider is leaning in.
🔴 Gross margin contracting while sports-rights costs climb; latest-quarter EPS down 49% year-over-year on the Super Bowl lap.
🔴 The thesis rested on a "fortress balance sheet" that no longer exists.

🟢 Genuine, large free cash flow (~$2.4 billion trailing) at a single-digit multiple — the deep-value starting point is real.
🟢 Tubi reached profitability ahead of plan; Fox One churn below expectations; both are credible, self-funded growth assets.
🟢 Two best-positioned ad verticals (live sports, live news) that are net beneficiaries of cord-cutting, not victims of it the way scripted-cable peers are.
🟢 Embedded sports-betting optionality (Flutter stake + FanDuel option) worth a stated ~$6–7 per share that the market does not credit.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important hidden signal is the **escalation of M&A language** described in Section 3 — management told you the cash was going to be deployed inorganically, and the market simply did not price the size or the target. A second, subtler signal is the **shift in how "distribution revenue" is defined**: starting in fiscal Q1 2026 the company folded Fox One subscription fees into the same line as traditional affiliate fees, which flatters the "distribution revenue grew 3–4%" headline by blending a growing new product with a declining old one. It is not deceptive — they disclose it — but it means the reported distribution growth overstates the health of the legacy cable affiliate business underneath.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** Fox is mid-transformation from a disciplined, cash-returning, focused-content operator into a content-plus-distribution-platform company via a large, leveraging, dilutive acquisition. The operating business is stable-to-strong; the capital-allocation posture has flipped.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** the entire deep-value case here was built on a fortress balance sheet and relentless buyback at a single-digit free-cash-flow multiple. That foundation was removed on June 15, 2026. Any position must be underwritten on the *post-Roku* Fox — higher debt, ~27% more shares in the float once the deal closes, free-cash-flow-per-share accretion that is years out, and integration risk against a platform (Roku) the market itself is skeptical Fox overpaid for. The cheapness is now partly a *deal-uncertainty* discount, not purely a legacy-media fear-print.

**Economic moat:** NARROW and, on the legacy side, ERODING. Fox's edge is an intangible-brand moat in live news (Fox News's audience is genuinely sticky and hard to replicate) plus must-have live-sports rights — both real, both why Fox is the *least* threatened legacy-media name. But return on invested capital is only about 10%, gross margin is contracting, and the affiliate base is shrinking 6–7% a year. This is a narrow brand-and-rights moat sitting on a structurally declining linear-distribution base, with returns that are decent but not widening. The Roku deal is precisely an attempt to buy a way off that declining base — which tells you management agrees the legacy moat is eroding.

**Secular threat:** MATERIAL (not terminal). The structural force is cord-cutting and the migration of viewing and advertising from linear to streaming. Fox is better positioned than any peer because live sports and live news travel to streaming with their value largely intact, and Tubi/Fox One are credible bridges. But the legacy cable-affiliate cash engine is in secular decline, and the Roku acquisition is a bet-the-balance-sheet response to it. The cheapness is therefore a mix of a legitimate fear-print on a cash-generative franchise and a genuine question about whether a $22 billion deal at ~2.8x leverage is the right answer.
